\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Dot product over the two-element field]
\lean{FABL.f₂DotProduct}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b002}
For vectors $a,x\in (\mathbb{F}_2)^n$, their dot product is $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i$ in
$\mathbb{F}_2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Additive maps over the two-element field]
\lean{FABL.IsF₂Linear}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b002}
A function $f:(\mathbb{F}_2)^n\to\mathbb{F}_2$ is linear if $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all
vectors $x,y\in(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$.
\end{definition}

Let $f$ be a map from the $n$-dimensional vector space over $br/2br$ to $br/2br$.
Then $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all vectors $x,y$ if and only if there is a vector $a$ such
that $f(x)=\\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i x_i$ for every vector $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Sign encoding]
\lean{FABL.signEncode}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b006

\label{FABL.signEncode}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.𝔽₂}
For $b\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, define its sign encoding to be $(-1)^b$ in the group
of units of the integers.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{1}
For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_2$, let the sign encoding send $c\in\mathbb{F}_2$ to
$(-1)^c\in\mathbb{Z}^{\times}$. Then the sign encoding of $a+b$ equals the product of
the sign encodings of $a$ and $b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sign encoding and the binary character]
\lean{FABL.signValue_signEncode_eq_binarySign}
\label{FABL.signValue_signEncode_eq_binarySign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.signEncode, FABL.signValue, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{3}
For every $b\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, the real value of the sign $(-1)^b$ equals the
binary character that takes value $1$ at $0$ and value $-1$ at $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Sign encoding of a function]
\lean{FABL.signEncodedFunction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p020-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001
}
\label{FABL.signEncodedFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signEncode, FABL.𝔽₂}
For a function $f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, define its sign
encoding to be the function from $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$ to the multiplicative
group of units of the integers that sends each $x$ to the sign encoding of $f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Real-valued sign encoding]
\lean{FABL.realSignEncodedFunction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p020-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001
}
\label{FABL.realSignEncodedFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.signEncodedFunction, FABL.signValue, FABL.𝔽₂}
For a function $f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, define its
real-valued sign encoding to send each $x$ to the real value of the sign encoding of
$f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sign identity for the BLR indicator]
\lean{FABL.two_mul_blrIndicator_sub_one}
\label{FABL.two_mul_blrIndicator_sub_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.signEncode, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_signEncode_eq_binarySign, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{5}
For $a,b,c\in\mathbb F_2$, let $(-1)^u$ denote the real sign associated with
$u\in\mathbb F_2$. Then
\[2\mathbf 1_{\{a+b=c\}}-1=(-1)^a(-1)^b(-1)^c.\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Sign of binary parity]
\lean{FABL.binaryParitySign}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p148-b004
}
\label{FABL.binaryParitySign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateSum, FABL.signEncode}
For a subset $S$ of the coordinate set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, define its binary parity sign
function on $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$ by sending $x$ to the sign encoding of the sum,
modulo $2$, of the coordinates of $x$ indexed by $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Closeness of functions]
\lean{FABL.IsClose}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b002
}
\label{FABL.IsClose}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.relativeHammingDist}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\beta$ be a set with decidable equality, and
let $f,g:\Omega\to\beta$. They are close at tolerance $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ when
their relative Hamming distance is at most $\varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Farness of functions]
\lean{FABL.IsFar}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b002
}
\label{FABL.IsFar}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.relativeHammingDist}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\beta$ be a set with decidable equality, and
let $f,g:\Omega\to\beta$. They are far at tolerance $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ when
$\varepsilon$ is strictly less than their relative Hamming distance.
\end{definition}

\label{FABL.exists_closestInProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.relativeHammingDist}

\begin{definition}[Closest function satisfying a property]
\lean{FABL.closestInProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b004}
\label{FABL.closestInProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.exists_closestInProperty}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\beta$ be a finite set, let
$f:\Omega\to\beta$, and let $P$ be a property of functions from $\Omega$ to $\beta$. If
at least one such function satisfies $P$, define a closest function satisfying $P$ to be
a function chosen among those satisfying $P$ that minimizes the relative Hamming
distance to $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closest function satisfying a property]
\lean{FABL.closestInProperty_mem}
\label{FABL.closestInProperty_mem}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.closestInProperty, FABL.exists_closestInProperty}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ and $\beta$ be finite sets, with $\Omega$ nonempty, and let
$f\colon\Omega\to\beta$. Let $P$ be a property of functions from $\Omega$ to $\beta$,
and suppose at least one function satisfies $P$. Then the function selected as closest
to $f$ among those satisfying $P$ also satisfies $P$, where closeness is measured by the
Hamming distance divided by $|\Omega|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Minimal distance among functions satisfying a property]
\lean{FABL.closestInProperty_minimal}
\label{FABL.closestInProperty_minimal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.closestInProperty, FABL.exists_closestInProperty, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ and $\beta$ be finite sets, with $\Omega$ nonempty, and let
$f\colon\Omega\to\beta$. Let $P$ be a property of functions from $\Omega$ to $\beta$,
and suppose at least one function satisfies $P$. For every function
$g\colon\Omega\to\beta$ satisfying $P$, the function selected as closest to $f$ among
those satisfying $P$ has normalized Hamming distance from $f$ at most that of $g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distance to a property]
\lean{FABL.distanceToProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b002
}
\label{FABL.distanceToProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.closestInProperty, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\beta$ be a finite set, let
$f:\Omega\to\beta$, and let $P$ be a property of functions from $\Omega$ to $\beta$. If
at least one such function satisfies $P$, define the distance from $f$ to $P$ as the
relative Hamming distance from $f$ to a closest function satisfying $P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Distance to a property is minimal]
\lean{FABL.distanceToProperty_le}
\label{FABL.distanceToProperty_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.closestInProperty_minimal, FABL.distanceToProperty, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set and $\beta$ a finite set, and let
$f:\Omega\to\beta$. Let $P$ be a nonempty property of functions from $\Omega$ to
$\beta$. For any $g$ satisfying $P$, the distance from $f$ to $P$, defined using a
closest function in $P$ and normalized Hamming distance, is at most the normalized
Hamming distance from $f$ to $g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment of distance to a property]
\lean{FABL.exists_relativeHammingDist_eq_distanceToProperty}
\label{FABL.exists_relativeHammingDist_eq_distanceToProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.closestInProperty, FABL.closestInProperty_mem, FABL.distanceToProperty, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set and let $\beta$ be a finite set. For a function
$f:\Omega\to\beta$ and a nonempty property $P$ of such functions, define their relative
Hamming distance as the number of inputs on which they differ divided by $|\Omega|$, and
let the distance from $f$ to $P$ be its relative Hamming distance to a chosen closest
member of $P$. Then some $g\in P$ has relative Hamming distance from $f$ equal to that
distance to $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Closeness to a property]
\lean{FABL.IsCloseToProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p031-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b002
}
\label{FABL.IsCloseToProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsClose}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\beta$ be a set with decidable equality, let
$f:\Omega\to\beta$, and let $P$ be a property of functions from $\Omega$ to $\beta$. The
function $f$ is close to $P$ at tolerance $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ if there exists a
function $g:\Omega\to\beta$ satisfying $P$ whose relative Hamming distance from $f$ is
at most $\varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[BLR acceptance condition]
\lean{FABL.blrAccepts}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p032-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b003
}
\label{FABL.blrAccepts}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
For a function $f:([1m[0m[1m[0mbf_2^n\to\bbf_2)$ and inputs $x,y\in\bbf_2^n$,
define the BLR acceptance condition to hold exactly when $f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)$, with
addition in the vector space over the two-element field.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[BLR acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.blrAcceptanceProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p032-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p174-b003
}
\label{FABL.blrAcceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.blrAccepts, FABL.𝔽₂}
For a function $f:\bbf_2^n\to\bbf_2$, define its BLR acceptance probability as the
probability that $f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)$ when $x$ and $y$ are chosen independently and
uniformly from $\bbf_2^n$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2$. The BLR acceptance
probability is the probability, for independent uniform $x,y\in\mathbb F_2^n$, that
$f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)$; if $F(x)=(-1)^{f(x)}$ and $\widehat F(S)=\mathbb
E_x[F(x)(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_i}]$ for each subset $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, then
\[2\Pr[f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)]-1=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\widehat F(S)^3.\]
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2$ be a function, and let
$\varepsilon$ be real. If the probability that uniformly chosen $x,y\in\mathbb F_2^n$
satisfy $f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)$ is $1-\varepsilon$, then there is a linear function
$g:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2$ whose relative Hamming distance from $f$ is at most
$\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Local correction rule]
\lean{FABL.localCorrection}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p033-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p177-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p182-b001
}
\label{FABL.localCorrection}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For a function $f:\bbf_2^n\to\{\pm1\}$ and inputs $x,y\in\bbf_2^n$, define its local
correction at $(x,y)$ to be $f(y)f(x+y)$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{5}
Let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be within relative Hamming distance at most
$\varepsilon$ of the sign-valued parity function associated with a set
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. For every $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$, the fraction of $y\in\mathbb
F_2^n$ for which $f(y)f(x+y)$ equals that parity function at $x$ is at least
$1-2\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
